items.stem: Where is Siddhartha's garden before the city?
items.quote: a garden before the city by the river
items.why: His wealth now includes land.

items.stem: Under what kind of tree does Siddhartha sit in his garden?
items.quote: sat down under a mango tree
items.why: He sits alone to think.

items.stem: Which games did Siddhartha learn to play?
items.quote: He had learned to play with dice and on a chessboard
items.why: He learns the pastimes of the rich.

items.stem: In the dream, where does Siddhartha throw the dead bird?
items.quote: threw it away, out in the street
items.why: He throws it out without thinking.

items.stem: People came to Siddhartha when they needed money or advice.
items.quote: they came to him whenever they needed money or advice
items.why: People liked and used him.

items.stem: Many people were close to Siddhartha besides Kamala.
items.quote: there was nobody close to him, except Kamala
items.why: Only Kamala was close to him.

items.stem: Complete: “left the city, and never came ____”
items.quote: left the city, and never came back
items.why: He leaves for good.

items.stem: Complete: “he possessed a house of his own and his own ____”
items.quote: he possessed a house of his own and his own servants
items.why: He has become rich.

items.stem: Match each thing to what Siddhartha learned to do with it.
items.why: He learned the comforts of the rich.
evidence: to bathe in perfumed waters
to have himself carried about in a sedan-chair
to sleep on a soft bed

items.stem: Put these events in story order.
items.why: One dream leads to a whole new decision.

cards.text: He dreams of a dead bird

evidence: Of this bird he dreamt.
he felt encompassed by a deep sadness
Siddhartha went to the pleasure-garden he owned
Siddhartha left his garden, left the city

items.stem: What drink, which causes sloth, did Siddhartha learn to enjoy?
items.quote: to drink wine, which causes sloth and forgetfulness
items.why: His habits change in the city.

items.stem: How old is Siddhartha when he notices gray hairs?
items.quote: who was only in his forties, had already noticed, here and there, gray hairs
items.why: Age is beginning to show.

items.stem: Besides money and jewelry, what does Siddhartha lose gambling?
items.quote: lost a house in the country
items.why: His stakes grow very high.

items.stem: How does Siddhartha spend that night at home?
items.quote: had drunk much wine and gone to bed a long time after midnight
items.why: He tries to forget himself.

items.stem: Siddhartha sometimes dreams about money at night.
items.quote: occasionally dreaming at night about money!
items.why: Money now fills even his sleep.

items.stem: Siddhartha still hears the holy source murmuring close within him.
items.quote: distant and quiet, the holy source murmured, which used to be near
items.why: The source now sounds distant.

items.stem: Complete: “Like a veil, like a thin ____, tiredness came over Siddhartha”
items.quote: Like a veil, like a thin mist, tiredness came over Siddhartha
items.why: Tiredness settles slowly.

items.stem: Match each feature of the Buddha to how it was described.
items.why: Kamala longs to hear every detail.
evidence: how clear his eyes
how kind his smile
how peaceful his walk had been

items.stem: What does Siddhartha see when he looks up that night?
items.quote: When, looking up, he caught sight of the stars
items.why: Night falls while he still sits.

items.stem: Put the gambling cycle in order.
items.why: Each loss drives him further.

cards.text: He flees into a new game

evidence: so high and audacious were his stakes
forced his debtors more strictly to pay
whenever he found his face in the mirror at the bedroom’s wall to have aged
fleeing into a new game

items.stem: Why does Siddhartha squander money at dice?
items.quote: in no other way he could demonstrate his disdain for wealth
items.why: Losing shows his scorn for money.

items.stem: Why does he love the fear he feels while rolling dice?
items.quote: for in this feeling alone he still felt something like happiness
items.why: Fear is the only thrill left to him.

items.stem: Why does he force his debtors more strictly to pay?
items.quote: because he wanted to continue gambling
items.why: He needs money for the next game.

items.stem: Why does his life seem worthless to him after the dream?
items.quote: nothing which was alive, nothing which was in some way delicious or worth keeping he had left in his hands
items.why: He has kept nothing living.

items.stem: His mockery of others grows tired as he becomes more like them.
items.quote: his mockery had become more tired
items.why: Becoming like them dulls his scorn.

items.stem: He leaves his comforts behind because he is no longer hungry.
items.quote: he felt strong hunger
items.why: He is hungry, yet he lets the comforts go.

items.stem: Complete: “lost his patience when he was not paid on ____”
items.quote: lost his patience when he was not paid on time
items.why: Greed makes him harsh.

items.stem: Complete: “He smiled tiredly, shook himself, and bid his ____ to these things.”
items.quote: He smiled tiredly, shook himself, and bid his farewell to these things.
items.why: He lets go of his comforts.

items.stem: Match each cause to its result.
items.why: Each event pushes him on.
evidence: after each big loss, his mind was set on new riches, pursued the trade more zealously
Starting up from this dream, he felt encompassed by a deep sadness.
he felt strong hunger, and thought of his house in the city

items.stem: Order the steps of his thinking in ¶12.
items.why: Memory leads him to judge his present life.

cards.text: He recalls praise as a boy
He admits it has long been silent

evidence: when he had obtained praise from the Brahmins
“Go on! Go on! You are called upon!”
For how long had he not heard this voice any more
The name of this game was Sansara

items.stem: What does the new dress growing old suggest about his life?
items.quote: As a new dress becomes old in time
items.why: His life wears out bit by bit.

items.stem: “like humidity entering the dying stem of a tree” suggests what?
items.quote: like humidity entering the dying stem of a tree, filling it slowly and making it rot
items.why: The world rots him from inside.

items.stem: Calling the merchants' world “a dance he would watch, a comedy” implies what?
items.quote: a dance he would watch, a comedy
items.why: He was never truly part of it.

items.stem: He lived the world's life “without being a part of it.” What does this show about him?
items.quote: though without being a part of it
items.why: Inwardly he kept his distance.

items.stem: Asking whether owning a mango tree was “not as foolish game” suggests what?
items.quote: was it not as foolish game, that he owned a mango tree, that he owned a garden?
items.why: Possessions now seem a game.

items.stem: “envied them just the more, the more similar he became” shows what paradox?
items.quote: envied them just the more, the more similar he became to them
items.why: Becoming like them sharpens what he lacks.

items.stem: Siddhartha's disgust that night is aimed most of all at himself.
items.quote: But more than by anything else, he was disgusted by himself
items.why: Self-disgust is strongest.

items.stem: “something had died” suggests Siddhartha's body is dying.
items.quote: inside of him, so he felt, something had died.
items.why: The death is inward, not bodily.

items.stem: Complete: “being tired and yet excited, close to weeping and ____”
items.quote: being tired and yet excited, close to weeping and despair
items.why: He is near breaking.

items.stem: Order the stages of his decline in ¶5.
items.why: Decay comes before he notices it.
evidence: tiredness came over Siddhartha
Siddhartha’s new life, which he had started after his separation from Govinda, had grown old
disappointment and disgust were waiting
had become silent
